The Kidako moray Gymnothorax kidako exhibits life history traits typical of a large-bodied muraenid inhabiting rocky reef environments. Field surveys off the coast of southern Japan have documented that females attain a total length at puberty of 62.1 centimeters [Lp = 62.1 centimeters], while males mature at a considerably smaller size, reaching puberty at 47.4 centimeters [Lp = 47.4 centimeters] total length. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in size at maturity is consistent with patterns observed in other congeneric species and has been linked to differential reproductive strategies between the sexes. For a female of average pubertal size, the corresponding estimated body mass at puberty is 441.3 grams [Wwp = 441.3 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions developed for this species. An assessment of the gonadosomatic index (GSI) conducted during the peak spawning season at a stable water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C] yielded a mean value of 10% [GSI = 10%].

Growth trajectories reconstructed from otolith readings reveal that the species achieves an asymptotic, or ultimate, total length of 91.5 centimeters [Li = 91.5 centimeters]. The corresponding maximum body mass, representing the ultimate wet weight predicted for an individual of this asymptotic size, is 1.57 × 10³ grams [Wwi = 1.57 × 10³ grams]. Both values were estimated using length-weight relationships validated against a large sample of commercially landed specimens. Juvenile individuals, immediately following the pelagic larval phase and settlement into benthic crevice habitats, undergo a rapid period of mass gain. The wet weight at birth, representing the mass of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva, has been estimated at 0.536 grams [Wwb = 0.536 grams] based on an assumed egg diameter of ten millimeters, which is consistent with the egg size reported for the closely related Mediterranean moray Muraena helena.

Under a stable thermal regime of 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C], embryogenesis in Gymnothorax kidako proceeds relatively slowly, with yolk-sac larvae emerging from the chorion after 93 days [ab = 93 days] — a developmental period that is prolonged compared to many tropical anguilliform eels but congruent with the lower metabolic rates typical of temperate-zone morays. Following eclosion, the lecithotrophic larva remains dependent on endogenous yolk reserves before the mouth gape opens and first exogenous feeding commences. This incubation temperature reflects the average late-spring water conditions in the species’ primary spawning grounds. Using the same thermal conditions, mark-recapture and captive maintenance data indicate that the maximum recorded lifespan is 34 years [am = 34 years], positioning this moray among the longer-lived members of the Muraenidae at a temperature of 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C].

Reproductive anatomy and spawning periodicity have been investigated through histological examination of gonadal tissue. The gonadosomatic index of 10% [GSI = 10%] was recorded at 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. This interpretation is reinforced by the size distribution of oocytes within the ovary, which displays continuous variation from primary growth through vitellogenic stages, indicative of asynchronous oocyte development and group-synchronous spawning. The length at puberty for females, measured at 62.1 centimeters [Lp = 62.1 centimeters], represents the size threshold above which more than half of the sampled individuals exhibited clear signs of prior or ongoing reproductive activity, such as the presence of post-ovulatory follicles or hydrated oocytes.

Comparative life history analysis places the Kidako moray at the slow end of the fast-slow continuum for anguilliform fishes. The maximum longevity of 34 years [am = 34 years], derived from data at 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C], is accompanied by a substantial ultimate total length of 91.5 centimeters [Li = 91.5 centimeters] and a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 1570 grams [Wwi = 1570 grams]. In contrast, the 93-day incubation period (93 days) [ab = 93 days] under identical thermal conditions illustrates the trade-off between extended embryonic development and the production of a relatively well-developed, large-bodied yolk-sac larva with a wet weight at birth of 0.536 grams [Wwb = 0.536 grams] at a temperature of 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C]. These combined traits—late maturity, substantial body size, and considerable longevity—align with the ecological demands of a top predatory lifestyle in structurally complex temperate reef habitats, where stable prey availability and low adult mortality favor a K-selected life history strategy.
